paper.title_en: Rotational Phonons Activated by Magnetism as a Key Ingredient of Cuprate Physics
paper.abstract_en: Circularly polarized lattice vibrations carry angular momentum and can link lattice dynamics to collective responses in strongly correlated materials, particularly cuprate superconductors. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) reveals ubiquitous quasiparticle "kinks" near ~70 and ~40 meV in cuprates, often accompanied by peak-dip-hump (PDH) features, indicating strong coupling between electrons and low-energy bosonic excitations. However, the relevant phonon modes and the role of circularly polarized vibrations in these spectral anomalies remain largely elusive. Here, we investigate electron-phonon coupling (EPC) in hole-doped infinite-layer CaCuO2 at four selective hole dopings (12.5%-56.25%) using the Strongly Constrained and Appropriately Normed (SCAN) density functional with explicit magnetic interactions. At 25% doping, the magnetic phase exhibits substantially stronger EPC (lambda ~ 0.5), five times that of the nonmagnetic phase, producing kinks and PDH features over 40-80 meV, with self-energy magnitudes comparable to experiment. Oxygen rotational phonons dominate the coupling over 50-65 meV, while breathing modes play a lesser role; the rotational modes emerge exclusively in the magnetic phase. At 37.5% doping, lambda increases to ~1.6 due to strong coupling of low-frequency phonons near the Fermi-surface nesting wave vector, whereas at 56.25%, where Cu magnetic moments vanish, lambda decreases to ~0.4. The rotational modes carry staggered angular momentum that cancels in the unperturbed lattice; a time-reversal-breaking gyrotropic coupling on Cu sites lifts this cancellation, yielding a finite phonon thermal Hall conductivity. Our findings establish magnetism-enhanced EPC as an important ingredient of cuprate physics and identify rotational oxygen phonons as relevant to spectral anomalies, superconductivity, and the pseudogap thermal Hall effect.
